task.goal: Stabilize a community kitchen's volunteer rota when availability changes at short notice.
hard_constraints: There are 20 volunteers, two essential roles per shift, and no new paid coordinator.
Never pressure someone to disclose health or family reasons for absence.
Measure uncovered shifts, last-minute messages and fairness of unpopular shifts.
task.available_resources: Existing roster spreadsheet and a telephone tree.
task.expected_result: A resilient scheduling mechanism with a missed-shift fallback.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Rotating, explicitly accepted backup duty
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Assign two qualified primary volunteers to each shift and an explicitly consenting backup for each essential role. One backup may cover either role if qualified, but cannot fill both simultaneously. The mechanism is advance reservation of replacement capacity: an absence activates a known person instead of starting a search. Use the spreadsheet to record role qualifications, confirmed assignments, backup acceptance and contact order. Rotate the volunteer who maintains these entries; no paid coordinator is needed.

An absent volunteer need only say “unavailable”; reasons are neither requested nor recorded. The primary contacts the designated backup through the telephone tree. A replacement is confirmed only after explicit acceptance, with a clear response deadline. If the backup declines or cannot be reached, call a short, predetermined list of eligible volunteers once each. Declining carries no penalty. At opening, if either essential role remains unfilled, delay service or use a previously agreed safe closure procedure rather than operate without that role.

This needs enough willing, qualified volunteers to reserve backup capacity without exhausting the group. Backup duty restricts personal time, so record both duty and actual call-outs alongside unpopular primary shifts. Allocate future offers using those separate totals, within declared availability, with an opportunity to correct errors. With only 20 volunteers, frequent shifts or narrow qualifications may make adequate backup coverage infeasible.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare a short pilot with an equal number of comparable shifts using the current telephone tree alone. Record uncovered shifts at scheduled opening, shifts still uncovered after escalation, and individual last-minute calls or messages sent. Inspect each volunteer’s unpopular primary shifts, backup duties and call-outs, accounting for availability. Rehearse one simultaneous two-person absence. The mechanism is challenged if backups routinely cannot accept, contacts do not fall, or coverage improves only by concentrating unpopular work on a few volunteers. A small pilot can reveal operational failures but cannot establish long-term reliability.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Consent-based replacement and reciprocal swaps
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Keep the normal rota, but create a standing replacement exchange using the spreadsheet and telephone tree. A volunteer who becomes unavailable can offer either a straight replacement or a reciprocal swap of future shifts. The mechanism is to make an inconvenient assignment acceptable through voluntary exchange, drawing on differences in volunteers’ schedules rather than reserving standby time.

Record qualifications, preferred contact windows and optional future shifts people are willing to exchange. A rotating volunteer acts as the exchange contact for each roster period. The absent volunteer reports only the affected shift and role; no explanation is requested. The contact makes one bounded round of calls to qualified volunteers who have opted into replacement requests. Offers include the concrete shift and, where available, a proposed reciprocal shift. Nobody is assigned through silence, and the original volunteer is not required to secure a replacement personally.

Both parties explicitly accept a swap, and the contact checks that it leaves neither shift short of either essential role before updating the spreadsheet. Count the unpopular shifts actually worked, including replacements, rather than just the initial assignments. Offer future desirable assignments first to willing volunteers carrying a disproportionate unpopular-shift load, without overriding qualifications or availability.

The approach assumes that availability differs enough for exchanges to be useful and that someone can briefly maintain the record. It is weaker during widespread absences or immediately before opening. Set a cutoff: unresolved gaps receive one final bounded telephone-tree escalation. If both essential roles are not confirmed and present, delay or close under an agreed procedure.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Pilot the exchange for one roster period against a comparable period using ordinary replacement calls. Log uncovered shifts, individual last-minute contacts, exchange acceptance and unpopular shifts actually worked per volunteer. Inspect every accepted exchange for a newly created vacancy. Include a tabletop case where nobody accepts. The mechanism fails its initial check if swaps merely move gaps elsewhere, increase message traffic without improving coverage, or repeatedly place unpopular shifts with the same people. Seasonal differences limit conclusions from a simple before-and-after comparison.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Availability-gated service with a smaller, reliable schedule
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Make the number and timing of kitchen shifts conditional on confirmed staffing rather than keeping every advertised shift open and repeatedly searching for replacements. The mechanism is demand shaping: concentrate willing volunteer capacity into a feasible service schedule. This alternative is usable only if the kitchen can safely move, combine or cancel some service sessions; that flexibility is not established by the supplied information.

In the existing spreadsheet, collect availability and essential-role qualifications from all 20 volunteers without requesting reasons for unavailable periods. Publish a provisional rota, then confirm only shifts with two named, qualified volunteers who have explicitly accepted. Where staffing is thin, offer volunteers a choice between consolidating into another session or leaving the session cancelled. Keep a simple telephone-tree responsibility for notifying volunteers and affected service contacts. Rotate this administrative duty among willing volunteers.

Set a practical reconfirmation deadline before each shift. A newly vacant role triggers one bounded call round to eligible, consenting contacts. If it remains vacant, activate the published consolidation or cancellation plan early. A missed arrival at opening triggers a short agreed waiting and contact procedure, followed by safe closure if either essential role remains absent. Consolidation must not create unsafe crowding, food-handling problems or unmanageable demand at the receiving session.

Distribute unpopular operating times through voluntary rotation, tracking actual assignments relative to eligible availability. Record cancellations separately so that reducing service cannot masquerade as better coverage. This approach may reduce frantic messages and unreliable openings, but it cannot preserve service volume when volunteer capacity is insufficient.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: First replay a recent roster, if records exist, using its actual availability changes: identify which sessions the gate would have confirmed or consolidated. Otherwise run a tabletop week with plausible single and simultaneous absences. Then pilot only where service flexibility is acceptable. Compare with the fixed schedule on uncovered shifts, last-minute individual contacts and distribution of unpopular shifts. Also report planned versus delivered sessions and any displaced service demand. Reject the approach if apparent reliability depends on unacceptable service loss, unsafe consolidation, or shifting unpopular work onto fewer volunteers.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Cross-qualified volunteers and role reassignment
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Reduce dependence on particular people by increasing how many volunteers can perform either essential role. The mechanism is skill flexibility: when a replacement cannot perform the vacant role, a qualified volunteer already scheduled can move into that role and the replacement can fill the other. This addresses qualification bottlenecks; it cannot solve a shortage of people overall.

Use the existing spreadsheet to map the 20 volunteers’ verified role qualifications and availability. Identify whether either role depends on very few people. Invite willing volunteers to learn that role during ordinary shifts through supervised practice, provided the kitchen has someone competent to teach and assess it. Do not treat observation alone as qualification or bypass required certification. Training feasibility and any costs are unknown; proceed only where existing volunteer expertise and resources suffice.

For each shift, explicitly confirm two qualified people and record any valid alternative allocation of their roles. A rotating, willing roster keeper maintains the sheet. When someone reports being unavailable, ask only which assignment is affected. Use the telephone tree for one bounded round of replacement requests. Consider candidates for either role: for example, move a dual-qualified person from role B to vacant role A if an accepting replacement can perform B. Confirm both assignments before updating the rota. Nobody must explain an absence or accept a request.

For a missed arrival, use the same reassignment check and bounded calls with an agreed opening cutoff. If two qualified people are not present, delay or close safely. Track unpopular shifts actually worked and offer future assignments within availability to spread that burden; dual-qualified volunteers must not become the automatic recipients of inconvenient shifts.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: First inspect a recent roster, if available, for vacancies where a willing replacement could have covered the other role but not the vacant one. Otherwise rehearse that situation on paper. Compare fixed-role replacement with role reassignment using identical availability and qualifications. Then pilot for one roster period, recording uncovered shifts at opening, individual last-minute calls or messages, and unpopular shifts worked per volunteer relative to declared availability. Record training time separately. The mechanism is challenged if reassignment unlocks no additional feasible coverage, requires unavailable training resources, or concentrates unpopular shifts among dual-qualified volunteers. A small pilot cannot establish reliability during widespread absence.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Allocate simultaneous vacancies as one matching problem
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
When several gaps arise, collect replacement offers briefly and allocate them together instead of filling each vacancy with the first available person. The mechanism is to preserve scarce availability: someone who can cover several roles or times is assigned where fewer alternatives exist. This can prevent an early replacement decision from making another gap impossible to fill. It creates no additional volunteer capacity.

Use the existing spreadsheet to record qualifications, accepted assignments and outstanding vacancies across the 20 volunteers. A rotating, willing dispatcher uses the telephone tree to contact eligible volunteers who have opted into replacement requests. Each person receives one consolidated request listing relevant gaps and can offer any subset, or decline without explanation. Absence reports require only the affected assignment; health and family reasons are neither requested nor recorded.

At a short, published response deadline, the dispatcher considers the offers together. Start with vacancies having the fewest eligible offers, checking whether moving a tentative allocation would allow another vacancy to be filled. For small batches this can be done manually. Volunteers explicitly confirm their final allocation; offering several possibilities never means accepting several shifts. Existing confirmed duties remain fixed, and overlapping assignments are prohibited.

Among allocations covering the same number of shifts, prefer volunteers with fewer unpopular shifts actually worked, considering their eligible availability and stated willingness. Do not penalize declines. The approach requires some overlapping offers, enough time for a brief collection window, and a dispatcher comfortable checking the sheet. For an immediate missed arrival, shorten the window to the agreed opening cutoff. If either essential role remains absent, delay service or close safely under an agreed procedure.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Run a paper comparison against sequential first-acceptance calls using identical qualifications, offers and response times. Include two simultaneous gaps where one volunteer can cover either and another can cover only one. Also test a single gap and a no-offer case. Compare uncovered shifts at opening, individual last-minute calls or messages, and unpopular shifts allocated per volunteer. Then inspect one short live pilot, recording actual unpopular shifts worked. Reject the approach if batching adds harmful delay, produces overlapping commitments, or increases contacts without improving coverage. Paper examples demonstrate feasibility, not how often useful matching opportunities occur.

EXPAND.title: Cross-train to remove essential-role bottlenecks
EXPAND.proposal:
Make more of the existing 20 volunteers qualified for both essential roles, then use that flexibility to repair gaps. The mechanism is qualification flexibility: an absence that previously required a scarce specialist can be covered by a wider group, or by moving a dual-qualified person already scheduled into the vacant role and recruiting someone for their original role. Two distinct people must still cover the two roles; dual qualification never permits one person to fill both simultaneously.

Start with a qualification matrix in the existing roster spreadsheet. Identify which role has fewer available qualified volunteers and offer voluntary cross-training to people whose availability complements that shortage. This requires a competent volunteer trainer, time for supervised practice, and any certification the role legally requires. Record demonstrated competence before assigning someone independently. If training requires unavailable external funding or expertise, this option is not currently feasible.

For each published shift, record whether either assigned volunteer could switch roles. When an absence occurs, a rotating, willing rota contact checks both direct replacement and role reassignment before using one bounded telephone-tree round. Confirm every changed assignment explicitly. Volunteers report only that they are unavailable; nobody requests or records health or family reasons, and declining training or replacement work carries no penalty.

For a missed arrival, the same contact checks attendance and attempts replacement within an agreed waiting period. If either essential role remains unfilled, delay opening or follow the kitchen’s agreed safe closure procedure.

Track unpopular shifts actually worked against each person’s declared availability, and offer future assignments to avoid repeatedly relying on newly cross-trained volunteers. The approach addresses qualification shortages; it cannot solve absences when fewer than two volunteers are available.
EXPAND.experiment: First inspect recent gaps, if records exist: would an additional dual-qualified volunteer have enabled coverage with people who were actually available? Otherwise, rehearse several gaps using volunteers’ declared availability. Compare feasible repairs with the current qualification matrix and a proposed expanded matrix, keeping headcount and contact limits constant. Then pilot training for the identified bottleneck and verify competence through supervised role performance. Record uncovered shifts at opening, individual last-minute calls or messages, and unpopular shifts worked per volunteer relative to eligible availability. The mechanism is challenged if gaps mainly reflect insufficient people, training does not produce independent competence, or improved coverage concentrates unpopular work on the cross-trained volunteers. A rehearsal establishes feasibility, not reliable future acceptance.

EXPAND.title: Overlapping working shifts as an on-site continuity buffer
EXPAND.proposal:
Where kitchen sessions are consecutive or long enough for a staff change, overlap outgoing and incoming volunteers’ working periods. The mechanism is temporal buffering: a late arrival or sudden absence can be handled by qualified people already present while replacement calls proceed. During overlap, volunteers perform useful preparation, service or cleanup work. Each essential role must always have its own qualified person; one person cannot cover both simultaneously.

Use the existing spreadsheet to identify handovers where short-notice gaps commonly arise, then seek voluntary overlap commitments from the 20 volunteers. Record each person’s role, arrival time and latest agreed departure. An outgoing volunteer may leave at that time regardless of replacement success. Any extension requires fresh, explicit consent. Volunteers report only availability; reasons for absence are neither requested nor recorded.

Assign one willing person on each shift to check arrivals and start a bounded telephone-tree round if someone is missing. The overlap provides a defined search window. If two qualified people cannot remain through the required operating period, stop admitting new service users and follow an agreed safe suspension or closure procedure before the outgoing person leaves.

This requires adjacent working periods, useful overlap tasks and enough voluntarily offered hours. Moving existing hours into overlap must not leave opening or closing uncovered. It offers little protection for isolated sessions or simultaneous absences. Track actual unpopular hours, overlap hours and extensions separately, and review their distribution against volunteers’ declared availability so reliable people do not become permanent buffers.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare a small pilot of overlapping handovers with similar handovers on the ordinary rota. Record uncovered shifts and uncovered role-minutes, last-minute calls or messages, total volunteer hours, and each volunteer’s unpopular hours and extensions. Count suspended or cancelled service as a coverage failure. The mechanism fails its initial check if overlap merely moves gaps to opening or closing, regularly requires departures later than agreed, or produces no coverage improvement despite additional hours. A small pilot can establish feasibility, but cannot establish reliability against rare simultaneous absences.
